comparison: Both support the behavioral model showing chronic stress induces depression-like behaviors (C1-C4). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers accept the core finding but request language changes to avoid anthropomorphization. OpenEval also evaluates C5-C6 separately (R2), while peer review groups all behavioral claims together.

OpenEval supports the use of TST/FST as validated depression models (C5-C6) based on literature citations. Peer reviewers accept this but request terminology changes to avoid calling behaviors 'mental depression.' Both agree on the validity of the behavioral assays.

Both address c-Fos expression in DCN (C7-C11). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers request additional analysis including presentation of absolute numbers (not just percentages) and clarification of cell type identification. The core finding is not disputed but data presentation is deemed incomplete.

Both address cell type identification of c-Fos-positive neurons (C12-C15). OpenEval supports the inference that these are glutamatergic neurons based on NeuN+/GAD67- staining. Peer reviewer 3 specifically asks 'what kind of cells were stained?' indicating this needs better clarification, though the approach is not fundamentally challenged.

Both address temporal dynamics of c-Fos expression (C16-C21). OpenEval finds the time-course data well-supported with dose-response relationship. Peer reviewer 2 raises significant concerns that c-Fos 'appears to be non-specific regardless of when the mouse undergoes restraint' and questions whether the temporal pattern is consistent with the proposed encoding mechanism. Major disagreement on interpretation.

OpenEval supports the speculation about DCN involvement in stress responses (C22-C25) as reasonable given correlational data. Peer reviewer 2's concerns about temporal dynamics (R3) indirectly challenge this speculation, questioning whether DCN activity patterns are consistent with the proposed role.

Both address PC activation effects (C26-C29). OpenEval supports the chemogenetic validation with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers raise critical concerns about interpretation, noting that manipulations during stress only address development (not expression) of behaviors, requiring language modifications. Disagreement on mechanistic interpretation.

Both address control experiments for CNO effects (C30-C32). OpenEval considers these essential controls demonstrating CNO alone doesn't affect behavior. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this as insufficient, stating CNO could have stress-specific off-target effects and requiring additional controls with CNO under stress without DREADDs. Major disagreement.

Both address behavioral rescue by PC activation (C33-C38). OpenEval finds the data well-supported across two assays. Peer reviewers accept the data but require clarification that effects are on development (not expression) of behaviors due to timing of CNO administration. Disagreement on interpretation scope.

Both address additional controls for PC manipulation (C39-C43). OpenEval considers these essential for interpreting CNO specificity. Peer reviewers' concerns about timing and mechanism (R4) apply to interpretation of these controls as well.

Both address the conclusion that PC-DCN circuit regulates depression-like behaviors (C44-C46). OpenEval finds this well-supported by converging evidence. Peer reviewers accept the data but require clarification about development vs. expression of behaviors, limiting the scope of the conclusion.

Both address DCN projection patterns (C47-C57). OpenEval finds the anatomical tracing well-supported and consistent with literature. Peer reviewer 3 notes most projections go to red nucleus (not VTA) and requests discussion of RN function and ipsilateral VTA projections. Agreement on data but request for broader anatomical context.

Both address retrograde tracing from VTA (C58-C64). OpenEval supports the complementary approaches and controls. Peer reviewers request discussion of anatomical findings in broader context, particularly regarding red nucleus projections. No fundamental disagreement but incomplete discussion noted.

Both address monosynaptic connectivity from DN to VTA (C65-C70). OpenEval finds the TTX/4-AP experiments rigorous and conclusive. Peer reviewers accept this finding without challenge, with one reviewer noting the 'compelling data set using anatomy, physiology and multiple intervention approaches.'

Both address cell-type specificity of DN-VTA projections (C71-C75). OpenEval acknowledges Ih is not definitive but finds the approach standard. Peer reviewers accept this without specific concerns, though reviewer 3 asks about anatomical location relative to red nucleus.

Both address quantitative connectivity analysis (C76-C80). OpenEval finds the mGRASPi and electrophysiology data mutually reinforcing. Peer reviewers accept this anatomical and functional characterization without challenge.

Both address collateral projections to cerebellar cortex (C81-C86). OpenEval finds the anatomical tracing and controls appropriate. Peer reviewer 3 requests additional images showing GFP in whole cerebellar cortex to demonstrate specificity to crus I, indicating the anatomical specificity needs better demonstration.

Both address functional connectivity from PCs to VTA-projecting DN neurons (C87-C90). OpenEval finds the electrophysiology conclusive. Peer reviewer 3 notes color co-localization is unclear in images, requesting better visualization, but doesn't challenge the core finding.

Both address behavioral effects of DN neuron inhibition (C93-C95). OpenEval finds strong causal evidence. Peer reviewer 3 raises concerns about potential confounds from inhibiting anatomically adjacent neurons (e.g., IPN) that also project to VTA, requesting discussion of specificity.

Both address additional behavioral assays beyond TST/FST (C96-C99). OpenEval finds this strengthens the phenotype characterization. Peer reviewers' concerns about anatomical specificity (R8) apply to interpretation of these results as well.

Both address behavioral effects in SST and NSFT with DN inhibition (C100-C104). OpenEval finds the data support effects beyond immobility-based tests. Peer reviewers request discussion of potential confounds from adjacent brain regions, affecting interpretation.

Both address CNO-alone control experiments (C107-C109). OpenEval considers this an important control showing CNO doesn't affect unstressed animals. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this as insufficient, requiring additional controls with CNO under stress conditions without DREADDs to rule out stress-specific off-target effects. Major disagreement on adequacy of controls.

Both address DN neuron activation inducing depression-like behaviors (C110-C113). OpenEval finds this demonstrates sufficiency of the circuit. Peer reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about contradiction with prior literature (Carta et al. 2019) showing DCN-VTA activation is rewarding and increases social interaction—opposite effects. Requires discussion of methodological differences.

Both address control experiments for DN activation (C114-C118). OpenEval notes appropriate interpretation of Gq-DN-Sal effects. Peer reviewers' concerns about contradiction with prior literature (R9) apply to interpretation of these controls.

Both address occlusion experiments combining stress and DN activation (C119-C126). OpenEval interprets lack of additivity as supporting same-circuit mechanism. Peer reviewers' concerns about contradiction with Carta et al. 2019 (R9) challenge this interpretation, requiring discussion of timing and methodological differences.

Both address SST and NSFT results with DN activation (C127-C135). OpenEval finds strong support for sufficiency across multiple behavioral domains. Peer reviewers require discussion of why activation produces opposite effects compared to Carta et al. 2019, particularly regarding timing (during stress vs. during behavior) and approach (chemogenetics vs. optogenetics).

Both address persistent behavioral effects after CNO cessation (C136-C143). OpenEval finds this demonstrates sustained circuit-level changes rather than acute CNO effects. Peer reviewers' concerns about methodological differences with prior literature (R9) apply to interpretation of persistence.

Both address the main conclusion about proactive circuit regulation (C144-C145). OpenEval finds this well-supported by comprehensive evidence. Peer reviewers require substantial discussion of contradiction with prior literature and clarification of development vs. expression mechanisms, significantly limiting the scope of this conclusion.

Both address correlation analysis between behavioral measures (C180-C185). OpenEval finds this appropriately addresses concerns about motor vs. affective behavior. Peer reviewers do not challenge this analysis, which supports the interpretation that immobility reflects affective rather than motor impairment.

Both address body weight changes validating stress exposure (C186-C187). OpenEval finds this provides important validation with appropriate literature support. Peer reviewers accept this without challenge as a control measure confirming stress effectiveness.

Both address lack of body weight effects from circuit manipulations (C188-C189). OpenEval finds this demonstrates specificity of behavioral effects. Peer reviewers accept this as supporting the specificity of the circuit's role in behavioral rather than general physiological stress responses.

OpenEval supports the hypothesis about PC-DCN-VTA circuit involvement (C91-C92) as well-grounded in anatomical and functional data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this hypothesis statement.

OpenEval evaluates speculative mechanisms about proactive vs. cooperative roles (C105-C106) as setting up subsequent experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these mechanistic hypotheses.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about cerebellar involvement in depression (C146-C154) as well-supported by literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically don't evaluate background/introduction claims.
OpenEval evaluates background claims about DCN-VTA connectivity and VTA function (C155-C168) as providing strong rationale. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval evaluates summary claims about main findings (C169-C172) as accurately representing the data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these summary statements.

OpenEval evaluates concluding summary claims (C173-C179) as supported by converging evidence, with therapeutic speculation noted as requiring validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these concluding statements, though peer concerns about interpretation scope apply.
